reflectivity-and-radar-basics: TIER 1, from an independent expert review. The card 'Atmospheric refraction' states: 'The atmosphere bends the beam slightly toward the ground. Under a standard atmosphere, this is treated as an effective Earth curvature of 4/3 the actual curvature.' The two sentences contradict each other and the second is wrong. Bending the beam toward the ground makes it rise MORE SLOWLY relative to the surface; the standard model captures that with an effective Earth RADIUS of 4/3 the true radius (k_e = 4/3 in the beam-height formula), which is an effective CURVATURE of 3/4. 'Effective curvature of 4/3' says the ground falls away 33% faster, which would make the beam rise faster - the opposite of what refraction does. The source passage is itself loose here, so do not copy its wording. Either state it as an effective Earth radius 4/3 of the true radius, so the beam's height above ground grows more slowly than pure geometry predicts, or drop the 4/3 entirely and keep the qualitative statement, which is all the checkpoint tests.
satellite-imagery-channels: TIER 1, from an independent expert review, in addition to any other finding. 3.9 micrometres is the shortwave-IR WINDOW band (fog and low-cloud discrimination, fire detection, night-time cloud phase). It is not a water-vapour band. Operational water-vapour channels are about 6.2, 6.9 and 7.3 micrometres. The error was inherited: the source table has a spanning row 'Infrared: 3.9-7.3 um (water vapor), 8.7-13.4 um (thermal imaging)', and the previous draft converted a spanning table row into a channel definition. Do not repeat that reading of the table. The wavelengths are not needed at Division B: prefer to drop the numbers from the cards and the checkpoint stem and identify the water-vapour channel by what it senses. ALSO: the Dvorak checkpoint asks about comparing a warm eye with surrounding cloud tops, but the card teaching cloud-top temperature and intensity appears two blocks AFTER it. Teach it before you test it. ALSO: three of four checkpoints are the same 'match the question to the channel' item with the same choice set; replace two with items that require reasoning.
stuve-and-skew-t-diagrams: TIER 1, from an independent expert review, in addition to any other finding, and it is wrong in two separate ways. (1) MECHANISM: surface cooling produces a SURFACE-BASED radiation inversion. The severe-weather cap is a warm, dry layer ALOFT - an elevated mixed layer advected off high terrain, warm advection, or subsidence. The previous draft's sentence was lifted verbatim from the source's Convective inhibition article; a bad sentence upstream is still a bad sentence in the lesson. (2) DEFINITION: the lesson never states what an inversion IS - temperature INCREASING with height - and its checkpoint keys 'capping inversion' to 'a layer aloft in which the parcel is cooler than the environment and buoyancy is negative', which is the definition of a CIN layer, not of an inversion. CIN can exist with no inversion at all. Define the cap by its temperature-versus-height signature, say that it produces CIN without being the same thing as CIN, and re-key that checkpoint accordingly.
velocity-and-rotation: TIER 3, from an independent expert review. Two things. (1) The checkpoint asking for gate-to-gate shear uses the SAME numbers as the worked example immediately above it (-48 knots inbound, 39 knots outbound, 87 knots). It tests whether the student scrolled up. Use different values. (2) The lesson says 'A velocity couplet is a nearby pair of opposite-sign inbound and outbound velocities, often called gate-to-gate shear.' The couplet is the PATTERN; gate-to-gate shear is the velocity DIFFERENCE measured across it. The same lesson treats them as distinct in the worked example, so make the definition agree.
air-masses-fronts-and-drylines: TIER 3, from an independent expert review. The lesson gives the warm, stationary and occluded front symbols but never the COLD front symbol - a blue line with triangles pointing in the direction of motion - and the cold front is the severe-weather boundary. Add it. Also add, somewhere it fits, that a mid-latitude cyclone rotates counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere: a search of all 26 lessons finds the course never says so, and it is a near-certain test item.
water-and-terrain-influence: TIER 2 and 3, from an independent expert review. (1) The checkpoint keyed to 'Moist air is transported upward, and a narrow, intense precipitation band may form downwind' rests on a card that appears AFTER it; the reading before the checkpoint stops at 'deposited on leeward, or downwind, shores'. Teach it before you test it. (2) The lesson is a grab-bag - tropical cyclone ocean heat content, lake effect, orographic lift, and a Hawaii trade-wind rainfall card - with no through-line, and the Hawaii card is ordinary climate rather than severe weather. Give the lesson one argument: how water and terrain change where storms form and how strong they get. (3) Lake-effect snow is taught twice in this course, near-verbatim here and in 'winter-storms', from the same passages. Keep the mechanism here brief and let the winter-storms lesson carry it.
saffir-simpson-and-storm-surge: TIER 2 and 3, from an independent expert review. (1) The checkpoint stem describes a STORM-SURGE WARNING but its explanation reasons about a HURRICANE WARNING - two different NWS products. Make the explanation answer the question that was asked. (2) The Category 4 card has no damage descriptor: its entire detail reads 'This range is listed for the Saffir-Simpson wind scale', while every other category describes damage. Fill it in.
observation-networks-and-instruments: TIER 2, from an independent expert review, in addition to any other finding. Two distractor rationales cite facts that appear nowhere in the lesson: six-hour SYNOP reporting, and a 60-to-90-minute radiosonde flight duration. The keyed answer is right, but the feedback teaches by assertion from material the student was never shown. Either teach those facts or write rationales from what the lesson does say.
wind-shear-and-hodographs: TIER 2, from an independent expert review. A distractor rationale explains the Bulk Richardson Number, but BRN is first introduced in a block AFTER that checkpoint. Move the definition earlier or drop it from the rationale.
watches-warnings-and-safety: TIER 3, from an independent expert review. One checkpoint tests an arcane SPC internal threshold - that a Severe Thunderstorm Watch forecasts organized convection producing at least six total severe weather events. No student needs the number six, and it crowds out what is actually tested: watch versus warning versus advisory, and which office issues which. Replace it.
winter-storms: TIER 3, from an independent expert review. Step 4 of lake-effect development reads 'The vapor freezes and is deposited on the leeward, or downwind, shore.' Vapour condenses and freezes in the cloud; SNOW is what reaches the shore. This is the source's phrasing and it is garbled for a middle-school reader.
storm-types-and-organisation: TIER 3, from an independent expert review. A distractor references mammatus ('A cloud formation beneath an anvil that appears near sunset'), a term the lesson never teaches. Distractors should be wrong for a reason the student can see, not unfamiliar.
